content.text: {"primary_meaning":"A “fool” most commonly represents a morally and spiritually undiscerning person—one who rejects God’s wisdom and consequently lives in unbelief, wickedness, pride, or disobedience. In biblical interpretation, the term usually concerns character and relationship to God rather than low intelligence.","primary_basis":["Psalm 14:1; 53:1 — the fool denies God and acts corruptly.","Proverbs 1:7, 22; 10:23; 12:15; 14:9; 18:2; 26:1–12 — fools despise wisdom, trust themselves, delight in wrongdoing, and resist correction.","Psalm 111:10 and Proverbs 9:10 — true wisdom begins with fear of the Lord, providing the contrast by which folly is understood.","Matthew 7:24–27 — the foolish builder hears Jesus’ words but does not act on them.","Luke 12:16–21 — the rich fool trusts wealth and neglects accountability to God.","Romans 1:21–25 — those rejecting God’s truth become futile and foolish despite claiming wisdom."],"alternatives":[{"meaning":"An imprudent, careless, or unprepared person whose failure is chiefly practical rather than an explicit denial of God.","basis":["Proverbs 6:6–11; 22:3 — wisdom and folly contrasted through foresight and conduct.","Matthew 25:1–13 — the foolish virgins symbolize lack of preparation and watchfulness."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A wicked or morally corrupt person, with “fool” functioning almost as an ethical category synonymous with the ungodly.","basis":["Psalm 14:1–4; 53:1–4 — folly is linked directly with corruption and evildoing.","Proverbs 10:23; 14:9; 29:11 — fools delight in misconduct, mock guilt, and lack self-control."],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"A person judged foolish by worldly standards but faithful to God; this is an ironic reversal in which apparent foolishness may express Christian discipleship or divine wisdom.","basis":["1 Corinthians 1:18–29 — the message of the cross appears foolish to the world but manifests God’s wisdom.","1 Corinthians 3:18–20 — one must become “a fool” by worldly standards to become wise.","1 Corinthians 4:10 — the apostles are described ironically as “fools for Christ.”"],"prominence":"common"},{"meaning":"An insulting designation for another person, emphasizing contempt rather than serving as a stable symbol.","basis":["Matthew 5:22 — calling another person “fool” is treated as culpable contempt.","Matthew 23:17, 19 — Jesus uses “blind fools” in prophetic denunciation of religious leaders."],"prominence":"minority"},{"meaning":"A literary counterpart to the wise person in wisdom literature, representing one pole in a pedagogical contrast rather than a single theological symbol.","basis":["Proverbs 1–9 — wisdom and folly are repeatedly personified or contrasted.","Ecclesiastes 2:12–16; 10:1–15 — the wise and the fool serve as contrasting literary types."],"prominence":"common"}],"has_settled_consensus":false,"confidence":"high","notes":"There is a strong broad consensus that biblical folly is primarily moral and spiritual, not intellectual. However, “fool” is not a fixed symbol with one meaning in every passage; its force varies among godlessness, wickedness, resistance to instruction, practical imprudence, unpreparedness, contemptuous labeling, and Paul’s ironic reversal of worldly wisdom."}
